content.html:
Core Concept›Universal Packages

What are Universal Packages?

Flexible, Schema-Agnostic Artifact Storage in Azure Artifacts

Definition

Universal Packages are a flexible package type within Azure Artifacts designed to store any kind of file or folder structure. They are schema-agnostic, meaning they don't enforce specific formats like NuGet or npm, and are essentially versioned, optimized archives.

Key Benefits

  • Versatility: Store any file type, from binaries to scripts.
  • Versioning: Track changes and retrieve specific versions reliably.
  • Immutability: Once published, a package version cannot be altered.
  • Access Control: Manage permissions for who can publish/consume.
  • Retention Policies: Automatically clean up old or unused packages.

Common Examples

  • Application installers (.msi, .deb)
  • Configuration bundles (JSON, XML, .env files)
  • Machine learning models and datasets
  • Large executable files or data sets
  • Infrastructure as Code (IaC) templates
  • Deployment scripts (PowerShell, Bash)
Why it Matters

Universal Packages centralize all your build outputs, eliminating ad-hoc storage solutions and bringing consistency to your artifact management strategy across the entire organization.

screens.title: Publishing Universal Packages

To publish a Universal Package, you'll use the az artifacts universal publish command. This command is your gateway to uploading any collection of files or folders into an Azure Artifacts feed. It requires several key parameters: first, the --organization which specifies your Azure DevOps organization URL; second, the --feed name where your package will be stored; third, the --name you want to give your package, which should be unique within the feed; fourth, the --version which is crucial for traceability and immutability, often tied to your build number; and finally, the --path to the local directory containing the files you wish to package. The contents of this specified directory will be compressed and uploaded as a single, versioned Universal Package. This process ensures that all your diverse build outputs are consistently managed, versioned, and secured within Azure Artifacts, just like your traditional code packages. It's a straightforward yet powerful way to bring order to your artifact ecosystem. Process Flow›Publishing

Publishing Universal Packages

Using the Azure CLI for Artifact Uploads

# Azure CLI command to publish a Universal Package
az artifacts universal publish 
  --organization <YourOrgUrl> 
  --feed <FeedName> 
  --name <PackageName> 
  --version <PackageVersion> 
  --path <PathToContentDirectory> 
  --description "Optional package description"
Key Parameters

Understand the essential arguments for the publish command to ensure your package is correctly uploaded and versioned.

Key Takeaway

The az artifacts universal publish command is central to uploading any file or folder structure as a versioned Universal Package to Azure Artifacts.

Parameter Breakdown

  • --organization: Your Azure DevOps organization URL.
  • --feed: The target Azure Artifacts feed name.
  • --name: The unique name for your Universal Package.
  • --version: A semantic version (e.g., 1.0.0) or dynamic (e.g., 1.0.$(Build.BuildId)).
  • --path: Local directory containing files to be packaged.
  • --description: Optional, but recommended for clarity.
Pro Tip

Always use a consistent versioning scheme, often integrating the build number, to ensure traceability and easy retrieval of specific package states.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough›Publishing Pipeline

Automating Universal Package Publishing

Integrating az artifacts universal publish into Azure Pipelines

# azure-pipelines.yml (Publishing Universal Package)
trigger:
- main

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

variables:
  universalPackageFeed: 'MyOrgUniversalFeed'
  universalPackageName: 'MyAppInstallers'
  universalPackageVersion: '1.0.$(Build.BuildId)'

steps:
- script: |
    echo "Creating dummy installer files..."
    mkdir -p $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/installers
    echo "Installer for Windows" > $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/installers/MyApp_Windows.exe
    echo "Installer for Linux" > $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/installers/MyApp_Linux.deb
    echo "README.txt" > $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/installers/README.txt
  displayName: 'Prepare Universal Package content'

- task: AzureCLI@2
  displayName: 'Publish Universal Package to Azure Artifacts'
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'YourAzureServiceConnection'
    scriptType: 'bash'
    scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
    inlineScript: |
      az artifacts universal publish \
        --organization $(System.CollectionUri) \
        --feed $(universalPackageFeed) \
        --name $(universalPackageName) \
        --version $(universalPackageVersion) \
        --path $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/installers \
        --description "Installer package for MyApp, build $(Build.BuildId)"

Pipeline Breakdown

  • Variables: Define feed, package name, and dynamic version.
  • Prepare Content: A script to create or stage the files for the package.
  • AzureCLI@2 Task: Executes the az artifacts universal publish command.
  • Service Connection: Requires an Azure Resource Manager connection with 'Contributor' role on the feed.
Key Takeaway

Azure Pipelines can automate Universal Package publishing using the AzureCLI@2 task, ensuring consistent versioning and deployment of diverse artifacts.

Real-world Connection

This pattern is ideal for publishing application installers, configuration bundles, or machine learning models directly from your CI pipeline.

screens.title: Avoiding Publishing Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When publishing Universal Packages, two common mistakes can lead to frustrating failures. The first is forgetting to specify the --path correctly, or providing a path to a directory that either doesn't exist or is empty. The az artifacts universal publish command expects a valid, populated directory to compress and upload. If the path is wrong, the command won't find any content, resulting in an error. Always double-check your staging directory and ensure it contains the files you intend to package. The second common pitfall relates to permissions. The Azure Service Connection used by your Azure CLI@2 task must have sufficient permissions to publish to the target Azure Artifacts feed. Specifically, it needs the 'Contributor' role on the feed. Without this, the CLI command will be denied access, and your package won't be uploaded. Regularly review your service connection's permissions and ensure they align with the actions your pipeline needs to perform. Addressing these two points proactively will save you significant troubleshooting time and ensure a smooth publishing process for your Universal Packages. content.html:
Pro Tip›Publishing Mistakes

Avoiding Publishing Pitfalls

Ensuring Successful Universal Package Uploads

Common Mistake 1: Incorrect Path

  • Issue: The --path specified for az artifacts universal publish is wrong, or the directory is empty.
  • Result: Command fails to find content, package not uploaded.
  • Solution: Verify the directory exists and contains the intended files. Use ls -l <path> in a preceding script step to confirm.

Common Mistake 2: Insufficient Permissions

  • Issue: The Azure Service Connection lacks 'Contributor' role on the Azure Artifacts feed.
  • Result: Access denied error, package upload fails.
  • Solution: Grant the service connection 'Contributor' role on the target feed in Azure DevOps Project Settings > Artifacts > Feeds > Permissions.

Best Practices

  • Pre-check Paths: Add a script step before publishing to confirm the content directory exists and is not empty.
  • Least Privilege: While 'Contributor' is needed for publishing, ensure the service connection has only the necessary permissions.
  • Error Logging: Configure pipelines to log detailed errors to quickly diagnose issues.
  • Test Permissions: Perform a manual publish with the service principal to confirm permissions before pipeline integration.
Key Takeaway

Proactive validation of package content paths and ensuring correct service connection permissions are critical steps for reliable Universal Package publishing.

Consuming Universal Packages

Downloading Artifacts with the Azure CLI

az artifacts universal download 
  --organization <YourOrgUrl> 
  --feed <FeedName> 
  --name <PackageName> 
  --version <PackageVersion> 
  --path <OutputDirectory>

  • --version: The exact version to download (e.g., '1.0.23456').
  • --path: The local directory where package contents will be extracted.
Pro Tip

For release pipelines, always specify an exact package version to ensure deterministic deployments and avoid unexpected changes.

It's important to ensure your Azure Service Connection has at least 'Reader' role permissions on the Azure Artifacts feed to successfully download packages. This integration allows your deployment pipelines to reliably fetch and utilize the exact artifacts needed for a release.

keyIdea.title: Automated Consumption
keyIdea.text: Downstream Azure Pipelines can reliably consume Universal Packages using the `AzureCLI@2` task, enabling consistent deployment and use of shared artifacts.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough›Consuming Pipeline

Integrating Universal Package Consumption

Downloading Artifacts in Downstream Pipelines

# azure-pipelines.yml (Consuming Universal Package)
trigger: none

pool:
  vmImage: 'ubuntu-latest'

variables:
  universalPackageFeed: 'MyOrgUniversalFeed'
  universalPackageName: 'MyAppInstallers'
  universalPackageVersion: '1.0.23456' # Replace with actual version

steps:
- task: AzureCLI@2
  displayName: 'Download Universal Package from Azure Artifacts'
  inputs:
    azureSubscription: 'YourAzureServiceConnection'
    scriptType: 'bash'
    scriptLocation: 'inlineScript'
    inlineScript: |
      az artifacts universal download \
        --organization $(System.CollectionUri) \
        --feed $(universalPackageFeed) \
        --name $(universalPackageName) \
        --version $(universalPackageVersion) \
        --path $(Agent.TempDirectory)/downloaded_installers

- script: |
    echo "Downloaded files:"
    ls -l $(Agent.TempDirectory)/downloaded_installers
    cat $(Agent.TempDirectory)/downloaded_installers/README.txt
  displayName: 'Verify downloaded content'

Pipeline Breakdown

  • Trigger: Set to none for manual or external triggers (e.g., release pipeline).
  • Variables: Define feed, package name, and the specific version to download.
  • AzureCLI@2 Task: Executes the az artifacts universal download command.
  • Verify Content: A script step to confirm the package contents were downloaded correctly.
  • Permissions: Service connection needs 'Reader' role on the Azure Artifacts feed.
Key Takeaway

Downstream Azure Pipelines can reliably consume Universal Packages using the AzureCLI@2 task, enabling consistent deployment and use of shared artifacts.

content.html:
Core Concept›Generic Artifacts

Generic File Artifacts in Azure Pipelines

Simple Build Outputs for Immediate Pipeline Context

Definition

Generic File Artifacts are any files or folders published directly from a build pipeline to Azure Pipelines' internal artifact storage. They are tied to a specific build run and are not stored in an Azure Artifacts feed.

Key Characteristics

  • Build-Specific: Tied directly to the build that produced them.
  • Internal Storage: Stored within Azure Pipelines' internal artifact storage.
  • Simpler Lifecycle: Retention is typically linked to build retention policies.
  • Limited Scope: Primarily for consumption by linked release pipelines or within the same project.

Common Use Cases

  • Compiled application binaries (e.g., .zip of a web app).
  • Test results and code coverage reports.
  • Deployment scripts specific to a single application.
  • Intermediate build outputs for immediate consumption by a release stage.
Key Takeaway

Generic file artifacts are ideal for simple build outputs that are only relevant to the immediate pipeline context, offering a quick way to pass data between stages.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough›Publish Generic Artifacts

Publishing Generic Build Artifacts

Using PublishBuildArtifacts@1 in Azure Pipelines

# azure-pipelines.yml (Publishing generic build artifact)
steps:
- task: PublishBuildArtifacts@1
  displayName: 'Publish WebApp Artifact'
  inputs:
    pathToPublish: '$(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/WebApp' # Path to your compiled web app
    artifactName: 'drop' # Name of the artifact
    publishLocation: 'Container' # Publish to Azure Pipelines internal storage

Task Inputs Explained

  • pathToPublish: The local path on the agent where the files to be published are located.
  • artifactName: A logical name for the artifact, used for identification.
  • publishLocation: Specifies where the artifact is stored. 'Container' means Azure Pipelines' internal storage.
Key Takeaway

The PublishBuildArtifacts@1 task provides a simple, effective way to store build-specific outputs directly within Azure Pipelines for immediate consumption by linked release pipelines.

After compiling a web application, you can publish its .zip file as a generic artifact, making it available for a subsequent deployment stage in the same release pipeline.

# azure-pipelines.yml (Consuming generic build artifact)
steps:
- task: DownloadPipelineArtifact@2

The DownloadPipelineArtifact@2 task enables efficient retrieval of build-specific artifacts, facilitating their use in subsequent stages or release pipelines.

screens.title: Universal Packages vs. Generic Build Artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the differences between Universal Packages and generic build artifacts is crucial for designing an effective artifact strategy. While both serve to store build outputs, their scope, reusability, and lifecycle management differ significantly. Universal Packages are stored in Azure Artifacts feeds, making them accessible across multiple projects and even organizations, depending on feed scope and permissions. They offer robust versioning, immutability, and advanced retention policies, making them ideal for artifacts that need broad reusability and a managed lifecycle. Think of them as a centralized, versioned repository for any type of component. In contrast, generic build artifacts are tied to a specific build run and stored within that build's context in Azure Pipelines' internal storage. They are primarily designed for consumption by downstream release pipelines linked to that particular build. While simpler to implement for immediate pipeline needs, they lack the cross-project discoverability and advanced lifecycle features of Universal Packages. The choice between them boils down to your needs: if you require broad reusability, versioning, and managed lifecycle across projects, opt for Universal Packages. If it's a simple output for a single build's deployment, generic build artifacts are sufficient. Choosing wisely ensures efficiency and scalability in your DevOps practices.

Comparison›Artifact Types

Universal Packages vs. Generic Build Artifacts

Choosing the Right Tool for Your Artifacts

Universal Packages

  • Storage: Azure Artifacts feeds.
  • Scope: Accessible across projects/organizations.
  • Reusability: High, designed for sharing and broad consumption.
  • Lifecycle: Managed by feed-level retention policies and views.
  • Management: Azure CLI (az artifacts universal publish/download).
  • Flexibility: Schema-agnostic, stores any file/folder structure.

Generic Build Artifacts

  • Storage: Azure Pipelines internal storage (tied to build).
  • Scope: Primarily tied to the build that produced them.
  • Reusability: Limited, mainly for linked release pipelines.
  • Lifecycle: Linked to build retention policies.
  • Management: Azure Pipeline tasks (PublishBuildArtifacts@1, DownloadPipelineArtifact@2).
  • Flexibility: Stores any file/folder, but less emphasis on broad sharing.
Key Takeaway

Choose Universal Packages for broad reusability and managed lifecycle across projects; opt for generic build artifacts for simpler, build-specific outputs within the same pipeline context.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to Chapter 6, where we'll dive into the powerful world of Universal Packages and custom artifacts within Azure DevOps. In modern DevOps, your build processes often produce more than just standard code packages like NuGet or npm. You might have application installers, configuration files, machine learning models, or even large binary assets that need to be versioned, stored, and distributed reliably. This chapter will equip you with the knowledge to handle these non-standard outputs efficiently. We'll explore how Universal Packages provide a flexible, schema-agnostic solution for virtually any file type, leveraging Azure Artifacts' robust features. You'll also learn to distinguish them from generic build artifacts and understand when to use each, ensuring your artifact strategy is comprehensive and effective. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to confidently manage all your build outputs, regardless of their type, bringing consistency and control to your software delivery pipeline.

As we embark on this chapter, our first goal is to clearly define what Universal Packages are and understand the significant benefits they bring to your artifact management strategy. You'll learn why they are a game-changer for handling diverse build outputs that don't fit traditional package types. Following this, we'll focus on the practical skill of publishing these packages. This involves using the Azure CLI, a powerful command-line interface, to upload your custom files and folder structures to an Azure Artifacts feed. Mastering this objective is crucial because it forms the foundation for centralizing and versioning all your non-standard artifacts, making them discoverable and reusable across your organization. Think of it as bringing order to what might otherwise be a chaotic collection of build outputs, ensuring every component is managed with the same rigor as your code.

Building on our understanding of publishing, our next objective is to master the consumption of Universal Packages within your Azure Pipelines. This is a critical skill for creating robust, automated deployment workflows, allowing your downstream pipelines to reliably access and utilize the artifacts you've published. You'll learn how to integrate the necessary commands to download specific package versions, ensuring consistency across your environments. Finally, we'll focus on distinguishing Universal Packages from other artifact types, particularly generic file artifacts. This objective is about making informed decisions: understanding when Universal Packages are the optimal choice for broad reusability and lifecycle management, versus when simpler generic artifacts suffice for build-specific outputs. This strategic understanding will empower you to design efficient and scalable artifact management solutions for any DevOps scenario. Advanced Artifact Workflows means learn to consume universal packages in pipelines and strategically choose between universal packages and generic file artifacts.. In practical terms, integrating universal packages into your pipelines. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Universal Packages are a cornerstone for managing diverse build outputs in Azure DevOps. Unlike specialized package types such as NuGet for. NET libraries or npm for JavaScript modules, Universal Packages are designed to be entirely flexible and schema-agnostic. Think of them as highly optimized, versioned '. zip' files that can encapsulate virtually any collection of files or folder structures. This means you can store anything from application binaries, configuration files, deployment scripts, installers, or even machine learning models within Azure Artifacts. The primary benefit of this versatility is that it allows you to leverage Azure Artifacts' robust features—like versioning, immutability, access control, and retention policies—for all your build outputs, not just code-related packages. This eliminates the need for ad-hoc file shares or separate object storage solutions for intermediate artifacts, bringing all your software components under a single, managed umbrella. It simplifies your artifact strategy, enhances traceability, and ensures consistent management across your entire development lifecycle, regardless of the artifact's content. The power of Universal Packages largely comes from their simplicity and ease of management via the Azure CLI. To publish a Universal Package, you'll use the az artifacts universal publish command. This command is your gateway to uploading any collection of files or folders into an Azure Artifacts feed. It requires several key parameters: first, the --organization which specifies your Azure DevOps organization URL; second, the --feed name where your package will be stored; third, the --name you want to give your package, which should be unique within the feed; fourth, the --version which is crucial for traceability and immutability, often tied to your build number; and finally, the --path to the local directory containing the files you wish to package. The contents of this specified directory will be compressed and uploaded as a single, versioned Universal Package. This process ensures that all your diverse build outputs are consistently managed, versioned, and secured within Azure Artifacts, just like your traditional code packages. It's a straightforward yet powerful way to bring order to your artifact ecosystem. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automating the publishing of Universal Packages within your Azure Pipelines is a common and highly recommended practice. This YAML example demonstrates how to integrate the az artifacts universal publish command into a build pipeline. First, we define standard pipeline elements like the trigger and pool. Crucially, we set variables for the feed name, package name, and a dynamic universal Package Version using $ open parenthesis Build. Build Id close parenthesis to ensure each build produces a unique, traceable package version. The script step then simulates preparing your package content by creating dummy installer files in the $ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis. This directory is a temporary location on the agent where artifacts are prepared before publishing. Finally, the Azure CLI@2 task executes the az artifacts universal publish command. Notice how it uses the defined variables and the $ open parenthesis Build. Artifact Staging Directory close parenthesis slash installers path. This task requires an azure Subscription service connection with 'Contributor' role permissions to the target Azure Artifacts feed. This setup ensures that your custom artifacts are automatically versioned and uploaded to Azure Artifacts with every successful build, making them ready for consumption by downstream processes.

When publishing Universal Packages, two common mistakes can lead to frustrating failures. The first is forgetting to specify the --path correctly, or providing a path to a directory that either doesn't exist or is empty. The az artifacts universal publish command expects a valid, populated directory to compress and upload. If the path is wrong, the command won't find any content, resulting in an error. Always double-check your staging directory and ensure it contains the files you intend to package. The second common pitfall relates to permissions. The Azure Service Connection used by your Azure CLI@2 task must have sufficient permissions to publish to the target Azure Artifacts feed. Specifically, it needs the 'Contributor' role on the feed. Without this, the CLI command will be denied access, and your package won't be uploaded. Regularly review your service connection's permissions and ensure they align with the actions your pipeline needs to perform. Addressing these two points proactively will save you significant troubleshooting time and ensure a smooth publishing process for your Universal Packages. Once your Universal Packages are safely stored in Azure Artifacts, the next crucial step is consuming them, typically in a downstream release pipeline or another build pipeline. Just like publishing, consumption is straightforward using the Azure CLI, specifically with the az artifacts universal download command. Universal Packages truly shine in scenarios where standard package formats like NuGet, npm, or Maven are simply inadequate. Their schema-agnostic nature makes them incredibly versatile. For instance, they are perfect for storing application installers, whether they're. msi files for Windows,. deb packages for Linux, or custom installer bundles. You can also use them for configuration bundles, versioning and distributing sets of configuration files for different environments, ensuring consistency. In the realm of data science, Universal Packages are excellent for machine learning models, allowing you to package trained models and their associated metadata for deployment. They are also ideal for large binaries or data sets that might exceed typical package size limits. Furthermore, for Infrastructure as Code (IaC) templates, you can group related ARM templates, Bicep files, or Terraform configurations into a single, versioned package. While Azure Container Registry is the preferred choice for Docker images, you could even store tarred image layers as a Universal Package for specific distribution needs. The key is their ability to manage any file type with the same robust versioning and access control as your code packages.

Beyond Universal Packages, Azure Pipelines also offer a simpler mechanism for managing what we call generic file artifacts. These are files or folders published directly from your build agent to Azure Pipelines' internal artifact storage. The primary task for this is Publish Build Artifacts@1. Unlike Universal Packages, which are stored in Azure Artifacts feeds and have their own lifecycle, generic build artifacts are tightly coupled to a specific build run. They are typically consumed by downstream release pipelines using the Download Pipeline Artifact@2 task. While less flexible than Universal Packages in terms of cross-project reusability and advanced lifecycle management, generic file artifacts are perfect for simple build outputs that are only relevant to the immediate pipeline context. Examples include compiled binaries, test results, or deployment scripts that are directly consumed by a linked release pipeline. They offer a quick and easy way to pass artifacts between stages within the same pipeline or to a directly associated release, without the overhead of managing a separate feed. Understanding this distinction is key to choosing the right artifact management strategy for your specific needs.

Understanding the differences between Universal Packages and generic build artifacts is crucial for designing an effective artifact strategy. While both serve to store build outputs, their scope, reusability, and lifecycle management differ significantly. Universal Packages are stored in Azure Artifacts feeds, making them accessible across multiple projects and even organizations, depending on feed scope and permissions. They offer robust versioning, immutability, and advanced retention policies, making them ideal for artifacts that need broad reusability and a managed lifecycle. Think of them as a centralized, versioned repository for any type of component. In contrast, generic build artifacts are tied to a specific build run and stored within that build's context in Azure Pipelines' internal storage. They are primarily designed for consumption by downstream release pipelines linked to that particular build. While simpler to implement for immediate pipeline needs, they lack the cross-project discoverability and advanced lifecycle features of Universal Packages. The choice between them boils down to your needs: if you require broad reusability, versioning, and managed lifecycle across projects, opt for Universal Packages. If it's a simple output for a single build's deployment, generic build artifacts are sufficient. Choosing wisely ensures efficiency and scalability in your DevOps practices.

It's your go-to for non-standard build outputs. Next, we have az artifacts universal publish, which is the Azure CLI command specifically used to upload and publish a Universal Package to an Azure Artifacts feed. This command is crucial for centralizing and versioning your diverse artifacts. Finally, az artifacts universal download is the Azure CLI command used to retrieve and download a Universal Package from an Azure Artifacts feed. This enables your downstream pipelines to reliably consume the exact artifacts they need. These three concepts form the foundation for effectively managing and distributing custom artifacts within your Azure DevOps environment, ensuring consistency and control over your software components.
